title: Particle Swarm
description: Track particles in 3D space to find the one closest to the origin long-term and count survivors after collisions.
writeup:
## Approach

The puzzle describes a set of particles in 3D space, each with position `p`, velocity `v`, and acceleration `a`. Every tick, acceleration is added to velocity, and velocity is added to position. We measure closeness to the origin using Manhattan distance.

The key insight for Part 1 is that, in the long term, acceleration dominates velocity and position. The particle with the smallest acceleration magnitude will tend to stay closest to the origin. If there are ties, velocity and position can be used as tie-breakers, but often simply picking the smallest acceleration (and then smallest velocity) is sufficient.

For Part 2, particles collide when they occupy the same position at the same tick. All particles at that position are removed. We simulate the system for a sufficiently large number of ticks until the system stabilizes (no more collisions and particles drift apart).

## Part 1

We parse each particle into `(p, v, a)` vectors. For each particle, we compute the Manhattan magnitude of its acceleration `|ax| + |ay| + |az|`. The particle with the smallest acceleration magnitude is the best candidate to remain closest to the origin in the long term. If needed, we break ties using velocity magnitude and then position magnitude.

The index of this particle is the answer for Part 1.

## Part 2

We simulate the particle system step-by-step:

1. For each tick, update all particles: `v += a`, then `p += v`.
2. Group particles by their positions.
3. Any position with more than one particle is a collision; all particles at that position are removed.

We repeat this for a fixed number of ticks (large enough that collisions stop happening and particles are clearly diverging). The number of remaining particles is the answer for Part 2.

This approach is straightforward and works well within the problem's constraints.
